 Republicans face a pivot away from Trump’s dystopia in 2028
 Analysis by Stephen Collinson 
 Updated Nov 20, 2026, 9:10 AM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 20, 2026, 12:01 AM ET 
 Getty Images/Reuters 
 Donald Trump 
 JD Vance

 Social media caricatures him as the man of many jobs. He’s been depicted as the Verizon Guy, the governor of Greenland and Manchester United’s next manager.
 But, in the parlance of Oval Office couch memes: Is “Marco Rubio realizing” that a new role now beckons — as a 2028 presidential candidate?
 CNN reported Thursday that some Republicans are quietly thinking about how to nudge President Donald Trump’s secretary of everything into the race. Many see him as the best hope of heading off another savage voter verdict on Trump’s presidency in two years’ time.
 New Rubio buzz followed the clumsy bid by presumed front-runner JD Vance to distance himself from the Iran war on the morning after the midterm elections .
 Rubio insists he won’t talk 2028. But he’s also not repeating his earlier line about not running if Vance does. And his steadying presence piped in from Manila about recent tech meltdowns made him look like a rare adult in the Trump room.
 Related article
 Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images, Sean Gallup/Getty Images, Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images, Eric Lee/Pool/Reuters, Alex Wong/Getty Images, Andrew Harnik/Getty Images, CNN 
 Everyone who might run for president in 2028 
 Speculation about the secretary of state and national security adviser — who also had spells as the acting head of the National Archives and acting USAID administrator — opens an intriguing chapter of the next presidential race, in which both parties will have open tickets.
 But Rubio — and anyone else who fancies the GOP nomination — has some hard thinking to do.
 Amid the wreckage of the midterms, a GOP hopeful might well wonder whether 2032 would be a better bet. It’s early, but Democrats are in the box seat because voters seem unlikely to be looking for a third term of Trumpism.
 Rubio is potentially intriguing. He’s managed to maintain a distinct political identity even inside the Trump maelstrom. This might equip him for the next GOP nominee’s most difficult mission: looking like someone new while running in Trump’s shadow. And Rubio has shown chameleon qualities by shedding his past as a traditional conservative hawk to enter Trump’s “America First” inner circle.
 STREAMING NOW
 CNN 
 Who’s pulling ahead in the 2028 presidential race? 
 Still, it’s a reach to think his Teflon act can survive association with Trump’s wild foreign policy and his deeply unpopular Iran war. If he became the Republican nominee, how would he answer Democratic accusations of complicity in policies like ICE’s street raids against undocumented migrants? And what would he say about Trump’s latest cozying up to his “friend” Vladimir Putin on Thursday?
 Rubio is also a willing member of an administration that permitted the world’s richest man Elon Musk, to desecrate USAID and deprive some of its poorest people of medical treatment and humanitarian supplies. Some independent observers warn this may lead to millions of deaths .
 Rubio also ran foreign policy while Trump threatened the sovereignty of Canada, one of America’s closest friends, and insulted America’s allies over their sacrifices in its post-9/11 wars.
 Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance attend a meeting at the White House on October 7, 2025. 
 Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters 
 Vance’s path looks increasingly difficult
 But if Rubio’s path looks daunting, Vance’s looks worse.
 His post-election critique of the Iran war might have appealed to members of the anti-war MAGA base who feel let down by Trump’s repudiation of his vow to fight no more foreign wars. But his social media post was maladroit, underscoring his own relative inexperience as a political campaigner: His Ohio Senate race in 2022 represented the only race he’s so far run in his own right.
 And Vance’s decision to embrace a Republican attack ad highlighting alleged child abuse suffered by Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton, which was widely regarded as the vilest such spot in recent memory, also raised questions about his political acumen.
 A presidential campaign is a relentless and exhausting two-year examination in which a candidate is always on and can’t afford mistakes. Vance made two big ones within the space of a few weeks, damaging his political stock.
 Still, the post of vice president does have advantages for an aspiring candidate. Air Force Two, official motorcades and a White House-level Secret Service detail convey the aura of the presidency and help voters see the veep in the top job.
 But history is daunting. Being a heartbeat away from the presidency and winning the job has proven all but impossible. When George H.W. Bush won the presidential election in 1988, he was the first sitting vice president to do so in 150 years.
 And Republicans like Rubio and Vance must ask themselves a key question: Where is their coalition? It’s not just a race to be Trump’s heir.
 “Trump’s base of support is uniquely un-inheritable,” Rick Tyler, the former spokesperson for Sen. Ted Cruz’s presidential campaign, said on CNN News Central Thursday. “So this idea … ‘Who is he going to give his base to?’ That’s not going to happen because Trump’s base is like fangirls. I mean, they’re just there for him. They’re for nobody else.”
 Rubio, with the experience of running his own campaign in 2016 and with the respect of various factions of the GOP, may have more unifying potential than Vance. There’s a chance that in a general election his profile might attract swing voters, especially if Democrats nominate a progressive candidate.
 Rubio’s dilemma in separating himself from Trump would pale in comparison to Vance’s similar problem. As vice president, Vance would need Trump’s blessing, but would also be forced to run away from the president to create his own political lane. That would be tough at any time. With the quick-to-take-offense Trump in office, it might be impossible.
 “The vice presidency is an unusual position,” Al Gore, who understands Vance’s position given his own unsuccessful 2000 bid to succeed President Bill Clinton, told CNN’s Dana Bash on Thursday. “And whatever power or influence a vice president has is almost entirely dependent on that which is granted by the president. The vice president has to work closely with the president. If that relationship is not good, then that’s going to be a difficult situation for JD Vance.”
 This could open a lane for rivals outside the administration.
 Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks at the National Building Museum in Washington, DC, on June 3, 2025. 
 Nathan Howard/Reuters/File 
 Rubio and Vance wouldn’t have the field to themselves
 Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, for example, has a demonstrable conservative record. His two terms were Trump-flavored. But he’d have the advantage of distance, having never served in the Cabinet.
 If Republicans crave a unifier, then Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox or former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin might work. And Sarah Huckabee Sanders could claim to be a Trump loyalist, as his first-term press secretary, but she’s sat out the mayhem of his second term while serving as Arkansas governor.
 But DeSantis would need to up his game after some awkward moments in his first presidential run in 2024. And the others are untested on the national stage.
 The 2028 nomination might look like a poisoned chalice now. But voters are in a volatile mood, and they’re yet to trust Democrats despite the massive anti-Trump vote in the midterms. And politics is so unpredictable that the nomination of a major party is always worth having.
 In presidential politics, timing is everything. If Rubio thinks his moment is at hand, he’d have to resign his posts fairly soon, since trying to run the world and a presidential bid are incompatible.
 Just maybe there’s an opening for a political athlete like Rubio, who has one foot on Trump’s half of the field and another in traditional GOP territory, with the nous to reinvent his party and engineer a positive pivot away from Trump’s dystopia.
 In Athens last month, Rubio seemed to test such a straddle, reviving the soaring, aspirational rhetoric that had him pegged as a potential president before Trump crashed the party. He backed the unapologetic use of American power but urged the reinvigoration of US alliances. He positioned the US as the steward of Western civilization dating back to Ancient Greece while lauding “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention.”
 Was that a signal? Maybe, since everyone’s suddenly talking about Rubio — including his boss.
 “How hot is Marco, right? Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic,” Trump said while addressing Southeast Asian leaders in Manila this week.
 Trump’s dire approval ratings mean his praise could be a blessing or a curse.
 But at least he didn’t praise Rubio’s “ass.”
